1.pericope_label: The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops? ... All thy rulers are fled together... Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people

schools.summary: Ellicott places the valley of vision in the lower city, in the Tyropoeon valley, where the epithet becomes still more appropriate, since that valley would be to the prophet in very deed a place where he saw things present and to come, and suggests the name grew more characteristic from the impulse given to the prophetic dreams of all who claimed to be seers. He sees the people in a state of excitement caused probably by the near approach of the Assyrian armies, keeping their revels on the flat house-tops that were a customary place of concourse; takes the joyous city for the characteristic on which Jerusalem, like Athens afterwards, specially prided itself; hears in the clause about the slain something like a reproach of cowardice, since those who perished had not died fighting bravely in battle but by the pestilence prevalent in the crowded streets of a besieged city; renders the third verse fettered without the bow, the rulers having ventured a sortie and been captured without a struggle; and hears in the fourth the tone of one who wishes to be alone in a sorrow too deep for visits of consolation. Delitzsch stands back from the chapter: the oracles on Babylon, Edom and Arabia are followed by this one, and the four were not composed in the tetralogical form in which they are grouped but joined at a later period on account of their close affinity, the internal arrangement suggested not by their dates of composition, which stand in the opposite relation, but by the idea of a storm coming from a distance and bursting at last over Jerusalem.

Gill takes the valley of vision for Jerusalem, lying in a valley encompassed with mountains, the habitation of the prophets and the seat of vision, and hears an allusion to the city's name, which signifies the vision of peace. He has the city full of stirs through the multitude walking about and the hurry of business, notes that the word signifies shoutings and acclamations and is used of joyful ones, perhaps those of the festivals, unless doleful ones are meant, and paints the streets clear, the shops shut up and all gone to the housetops for shelter; on the rulers he offers the civil and ecclesiastical heads, or the generals and officers of the militia, or the rulers of the cities of Judah who did not stay to defend them. Calvin gives the appellation to the whole of Judea rather than to Jerusalem, calls it a valley because it was surrounded on all sides by mountains, and thinks the metaphor harsher which makes Jerusalem a valley because it was thrown down from its loftiness; there is also an implied contrast, since valleys have less light than open plains because the height of the mountains intercepts the sun. He reads the flight to the housetops as disgrace: instead of being walls and bulwarks to defend the city, when there was no scarcity of men, they ignominiously turned their backs on the enemy, which urges the Jews to consider the judgment of God, since when such fear has seized the hearts of men it is certain that God has struck them with trembling. In the fourth verse he has the prophet assume the character of a mourner, bewailing the fallen condition of the Church of which he is a member, since what has befallen the Church ought to affect us as if it had befallen each of us individually.

Clarke maps the whole chapter before expounding a word of it: the prophecy concerning Jerusalem, the sentence against the steward, the prophecy concerning his successor, and then a transition from that successor to the Messiah of whom he was a type, agreeably to the mode universally adopted in the prophetical writings of making the things then present types of things to be fulfilled on a larger scale in distant futurity, with the sentence against the steward confirmed again at the close. On the third verse he finds an inconsistency in the received text, since if the leaders were bound they could not flee, their being bound standing prior to their flight in the construction of the sentence; he therefore follows a scholar who reads instead that they are gone off, a reading the old paraphrase seems to confirm. Wesley glosses briefly: the valley is Judah and especially Jerusalem, so called because a great part of it stood in a valley and because of the many and clear revelations of God's mind in that place; the housetops are where men went in times of great consternation, to look and cry to heaven for help; the noises are joyful shouts and the tumult comes of revelling and jollity; the slain died not in battle but by famine or pestilence in the siege, or in their flight; and the rulers are a later king and his chief commanders, bound in fetters.

Henry finds the title very observable. Fitly is Jerusalem called a valley, for the mountains were round about it and the land of Judah abounded with fruitful valleys, and by the judgments of God they who had been as a towering mountain should be brought low, sunk and depressed and become dark and dirty as a valley; but most emphatically is it called a valley of vision because there God was known and his name was great, there the prophets were made acquainted with his mind by visions, and there the people saw the goings of their God and King in his sanctuary. Babylon, being a stranger to God though rich and great, was called the desert of the sea; but Jerusalem, being entrusted with his oracles, is a valley of vision.

debates.question: Why is the place called the valley of vision?

positions.view: Jerusalem lay in a valley ringed with mountains and was the habitation of the seers; the name alludes to the city's own.
A valley because judgment would bring a towering mountain low, but a valley of vision because there God was known and his prophets taught.
Still more apt if the prophet's dwelling was in the lower city, where he saw things present and to come.
The name belongs to all Judea, ringed with mountains; the reading that makes the city a valley because cast down is harsher.
Judah, and especially Jerusalem, a great part of which stood in a valley.

debates.question: How does this oracle stand to the ones before it?

positions.view: The four were joined at a later period for their affinity, arranged by the idea of a storm bursting at last over Jerusalem.
The chapter divides into prophecy, sentence, promise and a typological transition to the Messiah.

debates.question: Why are the people on the housetops?

positions.view: Keeping their revels, in the excitement caused by the near approach of the Assyrian armies.
As men do in times of great consternation, to look and cry to heaven for help.
In ignominious flight, having turned their backs instead of manning the walls, which shows God had struck them with trembling.
For shelter, the streets clear of people and the shops shut up.

outliers.note: Emends the received text on internal grounds, since men described as bound cannot also be described as fleeing, and reads instead that they are gone off.
Turns the title into a comparison of privileges, setting Babylon as the desert of the sea against a Jerusalem entrusted with God's oracles.

themes: The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?
Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle.
All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far.
Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people.

5.pericope_label: For it is a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity by the Lord GOD of hosts in the valley of vision... And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield... And he discovered the covering of Judah

schools.summary: Ellicott divides the fifth verse between inward and outward, the earlier clauses painting the mental emotions of the coming day of judgment and the later letting us hear the actual crash of the battering-rams across the walls, with the cry of the panic-stricken people rising to the surrounding mountains, possibly as to the hills from whence they expected help, whether as true worshippers looking to Zion or to the high places which led their enemies to say that their gods were gods of the hills and not of the valleys. He names Elam and Kir as the chief elements of the Assyrian army then invading Judah, notes from the inscriptions that Elam was at this time subject to Assyria and conspicuous chiefly for its archers, and reports the identification of Kir with the region near the river Kyros, the modern Georgia, while granting there are both linguistic and historical grounds against it. He names the valleys that encircled Jerusalem on the west and south, filled with the chariots and cavalry of the invader ready to attack the great gate named in Sennacherib's own inscription; and on the covering he makes God the one who removed the veil which till then had hidden the approaching danger from the eyes of the inhabitants and laid bare their weakness to the invaders, adding that the verbs which the English version puts in the past are really a kind of prophetic present, painting the future as if actually passing before the prophet's gaze. Delitzsch describes the advance of the besiegers which leads to the destruction of the walls, without a word on who is responsible or why.

Calvin declares again that the Lord is the author of this calamity, so that the Jews may not gaze around in all directions or wonder that their enemies prevail, since they are fighting against God; and though the doctrine is frequently taught in Scripture it cannot be so earnestly inculcated as not to be forgotten when we come to practice, the consequence being that we are not humbled in the presence of our Judge but direct our eyes to outward remedies. On the sixth verse he breaks with the commentators he knows: they think the discourse proceeds without interruption and that the prophet makes known the same judgment he had just proclaimed, but examining the whole matter more closely he is constrained to differ, taking the passage as a reproach for obstinacy, in which the prophet relates the history of a past transaction to remind the Jews how utterly they had failed to derive advantage from the Lord's chastisements. Had it been a threatening, he grants, the future tense would have been proper, but the words immediately following are past. He will not fault the rendering a chariot of horsemen but translates literally, taking it for a military chariot, since two kinds were then in use, one for baggage and another for the field of battle; and on the covering he takes the verb indefinitely and the noun more simply than any of the others, as the armoury itself, so called because the weapons were not exposed to public view but concealed in a more sacred place. Gill hears the noise on the mountains of Media or on those bordering Chaldea, makes Elam the Persians who were then subject to the Assyrians and bore the quiver as expert bowmen, and takes the covering for the fenced cities of Judah, ruling out Jerusalem and the temple since neither came into the enemy's hands.

Clarke cannot see what a chariot of men should mean. The sentence consists of three members, of which the first and the third mention a particular people, so that the second should do so likewise; and since two Hebrew letters are so alike that mistakes arising from the likeness are frequent, he readily adopts the correction which reads Syria in place of man, thinking it extremely probable. On the arsenal he identifies the house of the forest of Lebanon as the building Solomon raised within the city, probably so named from the great quantity of cedar from Lebanon employed in it. Wesley says that not only men but God himself fought against them, that the walls broken are those of the strong cities of Judah, and that the crying to the mountains means outcries loud and dismal enough to reach the neighbouring hills; he makes Elam the Persians, then and long after subject to the Assyrian and Chaldean emperors, and Kir the Medes, named from an eminent city and region of Media; he notes that valleys were the properest places for the use of chariots and that the horsemen stood at the gate to assist the footmen in their assault and to prevent escape; and he takes the covering for the fenced cities which were a safeguard both to Judah and to Jerusalem, adding that their trust was placed in the arm of flesh.

Henry grants that what is meant by the covering is not agreed, and holds two senses together. The fenced cities of Judah were a covering to the country, but these being taken by the Assyrian army ceased to be a shelter, so that the whole country lay exposed to be plundered, and the weakness of Judah, its nakedness and inability to keep itself, now appeared more than ever; while its magazines and stores, which had been locked up, were laid open for the public use. A scholar he names gives another sense, that by this distress God would discover their covering, that is, uncloak their hypocrisy and show all that was in their heart.

debates.question: Is the passage prophecy or history?

positions.view: History: the prophet relates a past transaction to reproach them for not profiting by earlier chastisements, so the past tense stands.
Prophecy: the past-tense verbs are a kind of prophetic present, painting the future as passing before the prophet's gaze.
The chief elements of the Assyrian army; Elam subject to Assyria and known for archers, Kir doubtfully placed near the river Kyros.
Elam is the Persians, then subject to Assyria and expert bowmen.
Kir is the Medes, named from an eminent city of Media.
The middle member of the verse is corrupt and should name Syria, not man.

debates.question: What is the covering of Judah that was discovered?

positions.view: The fenced cities of Judah, which were its shelter until they were taken.
Both the fenced cities and, on another view, the uncloaking of the nation's hypocrisy.
The veil God removed, hiding the danger from the inhabitants and their weakness from the invaders.
The armoury itself, so called because the weapons were kept concealed in a more sacred place.

outliers.note: Emends the Hebrew from the three-part shape of the sentence, arguing that a middle member which names no people cannot stand between two that do.
Describes the besiegers' advance in detail while saying nothing of the theological question every other voice presses.

themes: For it is a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity by the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, breaking down the walls, and of crying to the mountains.
And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield.
And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate.
And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest.

9.pericope_label: Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many... but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof... And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping... let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die

schools.summary: Ellicott paints the hasty preparations for defence, matching the chronicler's account of a king who built up all the wall that was broken and added an outer line, identifies the city of David as the fortress of Zion and the lower pool as the Lower Gihon, and says the object of gathering the water was to stop the outflow of the streams into a reservoir, partly for the supply of the inhabitants during the siege but still more that the Assyrian armies might find little or no water in the immediate neighbourhood. On the numbering he says the houses were counted that some might be pulled down and others left as strategic plans determined, quotes what was probably a contemporary psalm bidding men walk about Zion and tell her towers and mark well her bulwarks, and notes that in a later siege houses were thrown down on account of the mounds employed by the besiegers. He would render the ditch a pond or pool to form a reservoir, identifies it with the pool known by a later name between two walls, and takes the old pool for Siloam or the king's pool. On the feasting he observes that the danger, imminent as it was, led, as in the plague at Athens in the time of Pericles and that of Florence in the time of Boccaccio, not to repentance but to recklessness and sensuality, and that the prophet echoes the cry of the baser form of epicureanism in all ages in tones of burning indignation; the closing warning, he adds, was borne in upon the prophet's inward ears as an oracle, and that sensual recklessness could have but one end, which was death. Delitzsch reduces the whole passage to a single point, that so far as the calamity had already proceeded it was a call from God to repentance.

Gill restricts the breaches to the stronghold of Zion, whose fortifications had gone to decay in times of peace and had been seen before without being noticed while the people were in safety, and insists that they are old breaches long neglected rather than damage newly made by the Assyrian army. On the numbering he offers four purposes without choosing among them: to know what number of men were in the houses and how many could be spared as watchmen or soldiers; to know how to levy the tax and what money could be raised; to compute how long the provisions would hold out; or to observe which houses stood in the way of repairing the walls and were proper to pull down, that their stones and timber might make up the breaches. He has the ditch hold rain water so that the inhabitants might not want during the siege. Calvin reads the whole as a study in how men behave, since during prosperity and peace no one cares about bulwarks or instruments of war, necessity alone arousing men and making them active while peace and quietness make us indolent and cowardly; so long as they thought themselves far from danger they disregarded the breaches, and only when a report of war arose did they grow anxious. He rejects the theory that the houses were numbered to supply watchmen and argues that the city was closely examined on all sides so that no house or building should be left undefended, which the following clause confirms, since houses built on the very walls in peacetime must be thrown down in war. The second clause of the eleventh verse is for him the point of the passage: they gave their whole attention to earthly assistance and neglected what is of the greatest importance, resorting to ramparts and ditches and walls instead of to God, in whom their highest defence lay. On the feasting he distinguishes: the prophet does not find fault with joy viewed in itself, since an apostle exhorts the godly to joy in the Lord, but censures the joy which is opposite to the sadness that springs from repentance, since it proceeds from brutish indifference.

Clarke describes the waterworks in detail: there were two pools near Jerusalem supplied by springs, the upper or old pool fed by one spring towards the higher part of the city near Zion and the lower probably fed by another towards the lower part, and when the siege was threatened the king stopped up all the waters of the fountains outside the city and brought them within by a conduit or subterranean passage cut through the rock, those of the old pool to the place where he had a double wall, so that the pool lay between the two. He reads the maker not of the pool but of the visitation, God being the author and disposer of the invasion with which he now threatens them, the very same expressions being applied to God on the same occasion in a later chapter. On the feasting he calls it the language of all those who have sought their portion in this life since the foundation of the world, quotes a Latin poem to the same effect, and reports that an emperor kept an image of death hanging in his dining-room to show his guests that as life was uncertain they should make the best of it. On the closing verse he notes that the Latin read a word for voice, without which he does not find the sense easy to make out. Wesley says the breaches were observed in order to their repair and the waters gathered both to deprive the enemy and to supply the city, that the houses were numbered so the people might exactly know their own strength and that those which stood on or without the walls gave the enemy advantage, and that the words long ago aggravate their sin in distrusting a God who had for so long given proof of his care in defending the city.

debates.question: Why were the houses of Jerusalem numbered?

positions.view: Four purposes are possible, and he chooses none: manpower, taxation, provisions, or which houses to demolish for the wall.
That some might be pulled down and others left, as strategic plans determined.
That no building be left undefended; the watchman theory others hold is wrong.
That the people might exactly know their own strength.

debates.question: Whose maker did they fail to look to?

positions.view: God, as the author and disposer of the invasion itself, not of the pool.
God, who made the city and the place of his special presence, and had defended it long ago.
God, to whom they should have resorted first instead of to ramparts and ditches and walls.

debates.question: What does the feasting under siege show?

positions.view: Recklessness rather than repentance, as in the plague at Athens under Pericles and that of Florence in Boccaccio's day.
The language of everyone who has sought his portion in this life since the world began.
A joy opposite to the sadness which springs from repentance, proceeding from brutish indifference.
That so far as the calamity had gone, it was a call from God to repentance which they refused.

outliers.note: Reconstructs the city's hydraulic engineering, tracing both springs, the stopped fountains and the rock-cut conduit, before touching the theology.
Reaches for the plague at Athens and the plague at Florence to explain why imminent danger produced revelry rather than repentance.

themes: Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool.
And ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall.
Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago.
And in that day did the Lord God of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth:
And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die.
And it was revealed in mine ears by the Lord of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord God of hosts.

15.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house... Behold, the LORD will carry thee away with a mighty captivity... And I will drive thee from thy station

schools.summary: Ellicott opens a chapter in the internal politics of the reign. The word for treasurer, literally companion, implies a position like that of a vizier, probably identical with the king's friend of the older histories, and in addition the man was over the house, an office like a Lord Chamberlain's and of such importance that it was sometimes held by a king's son, giving him supreme control over the treasury of the king and the internal affairs of the kingdom and making him almost a mayor of the palace under the Merovingian kings; his influence, Ellicott judges, was exercised to thwart the prophet's counsels, and he was prominent as the representative of the false security and luxury just condemned, and probably of the party which rested its hope on an alliance with Egypt. On the tomb he finds the prophet's indignation roused by a last act of arrogance: having no sepulchre of his fathers to deck with fresh stateliness, the man had built one for himself hollowed out of the rock, like the kings and great ones of the earth, to be his own everlasting habitation, and such rock-hewn sepulchres are found on the slopes of all the hills near the holy city. He would render the seventeenth verse will hurl thee with the hurling of a mighty man, that is, strongly and effectually, reporting a rival version that makes the noun a vocative, and prefers grasp to cover, so that thou shalt not escape; sees in the ball a picture of one flung violently on a smooth, even plain where it bounds on with nothing to stay its progress, taking the large country for the plain of Mesopotamia; and on the change of person in the nineteenth verse says that such changes are common enough in Hebrew prophetic speech, God being the subject of both clauses. Delitzsch prints the whole passage, from the question about the sepulchre to the calling of the successor, without a word of comment.

Calvin gives the man two titles, scribe or chancellor and steward of the house, noting that here he is called steward while a later chapter calls him scribe, which has led some to think that he had by then resigned the stewardship and that Eliakim was put in his room; this Calvin leaves uncertain, inferring only that the man cherished a wicked envy which led him to attempt to degrade his successor. On the sepulchre he asks why he built a splendid and costly one in a lofty and conspicuous place, as those do who wish to perpetuate the memory of their name in the world, and glances at the ambition of a foreigner and a stranger who longed to be so magnificently buried out of his own country while eagerly joining with enemies for the destruction of Judea: what could have been more foolish than to erect a monument in a country for whose ruin he was plotting? On the hurling he weighs the same options as Ellicott, since the noun denotes not an ordinary man but a strong and brave one, so that the sense becomes a mighty and powerful casting out, while others render it in the vocative as if the prophet were addressing him in mockery, O illustrious man, who so proudly vauntest of thy greatness and thinkest that thou art some hero; he prefers the first. He observes that a man so careful about his sepulchre, and who had given orders about it as if certain where he should die, is told he will not die in Jerusalem at all. Gill takes the questions as denials of any standing: the man is unworthy of such an office, an alien from the commonwealth of Israel with no estate or possession in the land; and he reports the paraphrase which makes the hurling the captivity of a mighty man, the Assyrian himself, together with the rabbinic observation that a man's captivity is harder than a woman's.

Clarke thinks the prophecy has very little relation to the foregoing except that it might have been delivered about the same time, and that the man may have been a principal person among those whose luxury and profaneness the prophet has just reprehended; he distinguishes this steward from the scribe of the same name in the later history, dates the prophecy before the invasion, and remarks that as to the rest, history affords no information, adding that two words are lost from the text and supplied by manuscripts and the versions. On the tomb he explains that persons of high rank in Judea and most parts of the east were generally buried in large sepulchral vaults hewn out of the rock for themselves and their families, and finds the man's vanity set forth by his being so studious and careful to have his sepulchre on high, in a lofty vault and probably in a high situation that it might be more conspicuous. On the covering he says it means the face, which was the condition of mourners in general and particularly of condemned persons. Wesley asks what right the man had to the place and office and what kindred he had there, reporting that the Jews say he was a stranger by birth, which he thinks the more probable because his pedigree is not mentioned in any place of scripture where he is named; he notes that the stately house to live in and the stately sepulchre to receive him are fitly joined together, since their sepulchres were commonly built in or near their houses, and that a rock was a fit place for both strength and state.

Henry finds the notice given to a single court appointment strange, since such changes are common in the courts of princes, and offers reasons for it. By the accomplishment of what was foretold concerning these particular persons God designed to confirm his word in the prophet's mouth concerning other and greater events; it shows also that as God has burdens in store for the nations and kingdoms abroad that are open enemies to his church and people, so he has for those particular persons at home who are false friends to them and betray them; and it is a confirmation in general of the hand of divine providence in all events of this kind, which to us seem contingent and to depend upon the wills and fancies of princes, since promotion comes neither from the east nor from the west nor from the south, but God is the Judge.

debates.question: Why does the oracle single out one court official?

positions.view: To confirm the prophet's word by a fulfilment on named persons, and to show God has burdens for false friends at home as for enemies abroad.
There is very little relation to the foregoing beyond a shared date and the man's likely place among those just reprehended.
A vizier and chamberlain with control of the treasury, thwarting the prophet's counsels and leading the pro-Egyptian party.
Steward here and scribe in a later chapter, who cherished a wicked envy against his successor.
A foreigner by birth, since scripture never gives his pedigree.

debates.question: How is the hurling of the seventeenth verse to be construed?

positions.view: Will hurl thee with the hurling of a mighty man, that is, strongly and effectually; a rival version makes the noun a vocative.
A mighty and powerful casting out; the vocative reading, which hears mockery in it, is the weaker.
The captivity of a mighty man, with the paraphrase: the Assyrian king himself.

outliers.note: Measures the office against the Merovingian mayors of the palace and reads the whole section as a chapter in the reign's internal politics.
Prints the entire section as a bare quotation, with no comment of any kind.

themes: Thus saith the Lord God of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say,
What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?
Behold, the Lord will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee.
He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord’s house.
And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down.

20.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah... And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder... In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed

schools.summary: Ellicott admits that nothing is known of Eliakim's previous history, but takes the epithet my servant as bearing witness to his faith and goodness, and thinks we may well believe him to have been in heart, if not openly, one of the prophet's disciples, holding at the time some subordinate office. The words about the robe point to an actual transfer of the insignia, a literal investiture, and father was perhaps an official title of the vizier, here indicating that the idea of the title should be fulfilled and the government be paternal in the truest sense. The key of the king's treasure-chambers and of the palace gates was the natural symbol of the office, solemnly laid upon the shoulder of the new official, perhaps as representing the burden of his responsibilities, and the same emblem reappears in the keys of the kingdom of heaven and in the custom of admitting a rabbi to his office by giving him a key. The word for nail serves both for the peg that fastens a tent and for a nail driven into a wall, and the context requires the second, a symbol of the support upon which others can depend, while the throne of glory beside it is another symbol of sovereignty, the pride of a hitherto obscure house. Not without a touch of irony he paints how many will hang upon that support, the glory or the weight of the next of kin, the remoter offshoots, and at last the vessels of small quantity, cups such as the priests used and flagons or earthen pitchers, the whole crowd of retainers. Alone among the voices he refers the removal of the nail in the last verse to Eliakim rather than to Shebna, finding a judgment for the misuse of the power just portrayed, and granting that no record of the fulfilment survives, so that either it was fulfilled or it did its work as a warning and the penalty was averted by a timely reformation. Delitzsch again prints the verses without comment.

Calvin cannot say at what time Eliakim was substituted, since a later chapter shows him steward of the king's house while Shebna was chancellor; he thinks it probable that Eliakim was afterwards driven from his office by the older man's stratagems, and that Shebna, having triumphed, was punished when his frauds were detected and, driven or banished from Judea, fled to the Assyrians and there received the reward of his treachery, as frequently happens to traitors. He turns the investiture into providence, since all the changes that happen in the world are directed by God, who girds kings with a girdle and ungirds them according to his pleasure, and recalls the witty saying current about the Roman emperors, that they were theatrical kings, because players who have laid aside the rank of a king presently become poor mechanics again. On the key he refuses the allegory that some spend much time upon, since the expression is taken from an ordinary custom by which the keys of the house are delivered to those appointed stewards, that they may have full power of opening and shutting; and by the house of David he understands the royal house, an expression customary because it had been promised that David's kingdom would endure. The nail he finds an elegant metaphor from which godly magistrates, few in number, ought to draw large consolation, concluding that God has not only raised them to that rank but confirmed and established them as by his own hand; and from the hanging he infers that God does not exalt princes to honour that they may live in indolence or gratify their own passions, since the office of a prince is very laborious if he discharges it properly. Gill takes the robe for a badge of office and its wearer for a type of Christ, sees in the key an allusion to magistrates who carried one on the shoulder or embroidered on the garment, and reads the nail as a nail in a wall on which things are hung, so that all the father's family would depend upon him and receive honour from him.

Clarke says that as the robe and the baldric were the ensigns of power and authority, so the key was the mark of office, whether sacred or civil, and cites a Greek priestess called the key-bearer of her goddess and a woman high in office under a great queen who bore the same title, noting that among the Greeks, as here, the mark of office was borne on the shoulder. On the nail he explains that in ancient times and in eastern countries the houses were much simpler than ours, and it was convenient and even necessary, and made an essential part in the building of a house, to furnish the several apartments with sets of spikes or large pegs on which to hang the movables and utensils in common use; these were worked into the walls at their first erection, the walls being of such materials that they could not bear their being driven in afterwards, and they were contrived so as to strengthen the walls by binding the parts together. He adds that a considerable part of the magnificence of eastern princes consisted in their gold and silver vessels, and that the targets and shields of beaten gold in the royal armoury were ranged upon pins worked into the walls in just this way. He takes the nail of the last verse for Shebna, a repetition and confirmation of the sentence already denounced against him, and observes that what is said of Eliakim is very remarkable and its literal meaning not easy to understand, probably pointing to the change of the Jewish priesthood and the proclaiming of the unchangeable priesthood of Christ. Wesley says the call is by God's powerful providence, that a peculiar robe and girdle were the badge of the office and the new man should govern with fatherly care and affection, that the key is the government itself with the power of opening and shutting, mentioned as on the shoulder rather than in the hand from some ceremony then in use, that the meanest of the family should receive a lustre from their relation to him, and that the nail removed at the last is Shebna, with the burden all those wicked officers who had been advanced and supported by his power.

debates.question: Whose is the nail that is removed in the last verse?

positions.view: Shebna's: a repetition and confirmation of the sentence already denounced against him.
Eliakim's: a judgment for the misuse of the power just portrayed, bringing down his kindred with him.

debates.question: What does the key upon the shoulder signify?

positions.view: The mark of office, sacred or civil, with Greek parallels in priestesses called key-bearers who also carried it on the shoulder.
The chamberlain's symbol, its burden represented by the shoulder, reproduced in the keys of the kingdom and in the rabbi's key.
An ordinary custom by which stewards receive the house keys; no allegory should be drawn from it.
The government itself, the power of opening and shutting, of which a key is a fit emblem.

debates.question: What kind of nail is meant?

positions.view: A peg worked into the wall at building, on which the household goods of an eastern house were hung.
A nail driven into a wall rather than a tent-peg, a symbol of the support on which others depend.
An elegant metaphor of stability, from which godly magistrates may draw large consolation.
The establishment of power in his hands, in strong walls or solid timber.

outliers.note: Contributes a second bare quotation in the same chapter, printing four verses of text with no comment attached.
Compares the promotion and fall of court officials to the Roman emperors called theatrical kings, players who become poor mechanics once the costume is off.

themes: And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah:

And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah.
And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.
And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father’s house.
And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons.

In that day, saith the Lord of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that was upon it shall be cut off: for the Lord hath spoken it.
